candidates.current_role: Chief Justice, Fifteenth Court of Appeals, since September 2024 (appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott)
candidates.background: Scott Brister is a Waco native with degrees from Duke University (1977) and Harvard Law School (1980), and he is board certified in civil appellate law, civil trial law and personal injury trial law. He presided over Harris County's 234th District Court from 1989 to 2000, served on Houston's First and Fourteenth Courts of Appeals (including as chief justice of the Fourteenth), and served on the Texas Supreme Court from 2003 to 2009. He was a partner at Hunton Andrews Kurth before Gov. Greg Abbott named him the first chief justice of the new statewide Fifteenth Court of Appeals.

priorities.text: Campaigns on establishing the Fifteenth Court of Appeals as a stable, principled statewide court.
Says he aims for consistent rulings in cases involving state government and business law.
Emphasizes clear legal writing and reasoned decisions.
Says every party deserves an impartial judge who applies the law, not personal beliefs or political preferences.
Campaigns on preserving public trust in the courts.

promises.text: Says he will follow the law as written and rule without regard to personal beliefs or politics.

record.text: Presided over the 234th District Court in Harris County from 1989 to 2000 and served on the First and Fourteenth Courts of Appeals from 2001 to 2003.
Served on the Texas Supreme Court from 2003 to 2009 after appointment by Gov. Rick Perry and election in 2004, writing 122 opinions for that court.

Wrote a dissent in the Texas Supreme Court school finance case Neely v. West Orange-Cove Consolidated ISD (2005), disagreeing with the judgment that the state's school finance plan was unconstitutional.
Chaired the Texas Commission on Public School Finance after a 2017 appointment by Gov. Greg Abbott.
Appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott in June 2024 as the first chief justice of the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, effective September 1, 2024.

Wrote the Fifteenth Court's August 2025 opinion dismissing Dallas County's suit against the Health and Human Services Commission over the backlog of mentally incompetent jail inmates awaiting state hospital beds; the Texas Supreme Court declined review in June 2026.

Filed a concurrence in December 2025 when the Fifteenth Court upheld an injunction blocking Attorney General Ken Paxton's reporting rules for large-county prosecutors, writing in substance that Paxton may request information in specific cases but may not impose blanket requirements.

notes.text: In the 1990s he posted the Ten Commandments in his Harris County courtroom and declined to remove them after being sued, according to the Texas Tribune.
The Fifteenth Court has ruled against Attorney General Ken Paxton in several high-profile cases, drawing public criticism from Paxton.

Bloomberg Law reported that he twice admonished lawyers from the attorney general's office over where and how the office files cases, including suits against Johnson & Johnson and Kenvue in small counties, and said both sides should be counseled toward professionalism.
State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll: Brister 1,957 votes, Jerry Zimmerer 1,594 (about 55 percent to 45 percent). The poll is a non-scientific survey of participating lawyers.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, State Rep. Pat Curry and Texas Alliance for Life, and by the Texas Civil Justice League PAC.
Reported $228,242 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; major donors included Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000).

q_textualism.summary: Says judges are not lawmakers and should follow the law as written and respect the Constitution.

issue_notes.summary: Has said the rift between the attorney general's office and the court is unhealthy and that both sides should be counseled toward professionalism.
